meta.title: Who really said "They say a tie is like kissing your sister. I guess that is better than kissing your brother"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The sister line is football folklore, first credited to Navy’s Eddie Erdelatz in 1953. The brother topper is Lou Holtz’s — on one unreachable citation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They say a tie is like kissing your sister. I guess that is better than kissing your brother'?
meta.ogDescription: Holtz says “they say” for a reason: he did not write the first half. Who did, and how good is the evidence for the second?

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1937–2026 · college football coach; Notre Dame national champion, 1988
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Holtz, and unchallenged — no other page on Wikiquote gives this line to anyone else. Holtz is only claiming half of it, and says so: “They say” marks the sister comparison as a saying he inherited, and Wikipedia’s account traces that half to Navy coach Eddie Erdelatz in 1953. The topper about the brother is the part that is Holtz’s, and the only citation for it is a listicle we could not open. Widely repeated, consistent with his style, not pinned to a primary source.

source.excerpt: “They say a tie is like kissing your sister. I guess that is better than kissing your brother.”
trail: Wikiquote ↗ files this line under Attributed, which is its own signal: the page has no sourced section at all, and every quotation on it carries the same kind of second-hand citation.

That citation is a Bleacher Report listicle, “Top 15 Funniest Lou Holtz Quotes” by Ben Weiximann. The host is unreachable from our network, so we can neither confirm what it says nor what it cites. We are not counting it as corroboration.

The setup is not Holtz’s and he does not claim it. Wikipedia’s article on the tie ↗ reports that the unpopularity of drawn games “is reflected in the saying, ‘A tie is like kissing your sister’” and that the earliest known use was by Navy coach Eddie Erdelatz ↗ after a scoreless tie with Duke in 1953. Its own footnote for that is an American Dialect Society list message held only in the Wayback Machine, which we could not reach — so we are reporting Wikipedia’s finding as Wikipedia’s, not as a primary confirmation.
The 1953 game is independently on the record: Navy’s 1953 schedule ↗ shows a 0–0 tie with Duke at Municipal Stadium in Baltimore on 7 November 1953, which is the match the attribution refers to.

A phrase search across the whole of English Wikiquote finds “kissing your sister” on three pages and “kissing your brother” on two; apart from Holtz, every hit is dialogue from a film or television series rather than an attribution to a person. Nobody else is claiming this line.
source.excerptNote: The words “They say” are doing real work here. Holtz is quoting a saying older than his own career and then capping it — so only the second sentence is a claim to authorship at all.

source.rightsNote: We cannot name a first publication for this line, so we cannot point you at a document. What we can say is that it is not in the public domain: Holtz’s coaching and broadcasting career ran from 1969 to 2015, and everything published in the United States from 1931 onward is still under copyright protection. Treat it as in copyright and quote it as a quotation, with attribution, rather than reusing it as free text.

author.name: Lou Holtz
author.heading: About Lou Holtz
author.metaLine: 1937–2026 · American college football coach · Notre Dame, 1986–1996
author.bio: Lou Holtz was an American college football coach who took six different programmes to bowl games and finished with a career college record of 249–132–7. His 1988 Notre Dame team went 12–0 and was the consensus national champion. He was elected to the College Football Hall of Fame in 2008. Much of his quotable reputation rests on this kind of line — a stock coaching saying given one extra turn — which is also why so little of it is traceable to a primary source.

misattribution.heading: Who the first half belongs to
misattribution.intro: This is a joke built on a borrowed line, and Holtz flags the borrowing himself. Splitting it in two is the only honest way to answer “who said this?”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sister joke was the standard American complaint about drawn games for decades, and it had a real target: college football allowed ties, and a hard-fought 0–0 counted for nothing much in anyone’s eyes. Erdelatz reached for it after exactly that kind of afternoon in Baltimore in 1953.
Holtz’s addition is a coach’s joke rather than a fan’s. It does not complain that ties are unsatisfying; it concedes the cliché and then finds something worse to compare them with.
detailsBody: There is a neat piece of timing behind it. Holtz coached Notre Dame from 1986 to 1996, and the NCAA introduced overtime in college football in 1996 — eliminating ties except for severe weather or curfew. The saying he was riffing on was on its way to obsolescence in his final season on that sideline.

It is worth saying plainly what this page cannot tell you: when Holtz said it, to whom, or after which game. Wikiquote offers no occasion and the one citation it gives cannot be opened from here. What we can establish is the shape of the joke, the origin of the half he borrowed, and the fact that no one else has ever claimed the half he added.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote’s Lou Holtz page lists "They say a tie is like kissing your sister. I guess that is better than kissing your brother." in its Attributed section, citing only Ben Weiximann, "Top 15 Funniest Lou Holtz Quotes", TheBleacherReport.com. The page has an Attributed section and no sourced section.

Wikipedia’s "Tie (draw)" article states that the unpopularity of ties in American sports "is reflected in the saying, 'A tie is like kissing your sister.'" and that "The earliest known use of the phrase was by Navy football coach Eddie Erdelatz after a scoreless tie against Duke in 1953." The same article states that in NCAA college football "overtime was introduced in 1996, eliminating ties except in the event of severe weather or curfew situations."
The 1953 Navy Midshipmen football schedule records a tie against Duke on November 7 at Municipal Stadium, Baltimore, MD, final score 0–0, attendance 15,000.
Eddie Erdelatz returned to Navy as head coach in 1950 after a spell as defensive coordinator of the San Francisco 49ers.

Lou Holtz (January 6, 1937 – March 4, 2026) was head coach at Notre Dame 1986–1996 with a career college record of 249–132–7, was consensus national champion in 1988, and was elected to the College Football Hall of Fame in 2008.
